lesson.title: Communication Links: The Physical Paths Between Nodes
lesson.summary: Defines the communication link as the physical or wireless medium connecting two nodes, covering guided versus unguided media and the concept of transmission rate.
lesson.body:
Every node in a network, whether it is a host at the edge or a router in the core, has to actually connect to something, and that physical or wireless connection is called a communication link. A link is the medium over which data travels between two nodes: it could be a copper cable, a strand of optical fiber, or a wireless radio signal passing through the air. Without links, nodes would just be isolated devices with nowhere to send anything. Every access link connecting a host to the edge and every backbone connection between routers in the core, both concepts from the previous two sections, is an example of a communication link doing its job.

Links are generally grouped into two broad categories based on how they carry a signal. Guided media physically confine the signal to a solid path, this includes twisted pair copper cabling, commonly used for wired Ethernet connections, coaxial cable, and fiber optic cable, which sends data as pulses of light and can carry enormous amounts of information over long distances with very low signal loss. Unguided media, by contrast, send signals through open space with nothing physically confining them, this includes WiFi, cellular data connections, and satellite links. Each category has real tradeoffs: guided media generally offer higher reliability and speed but require physical installation, while unguided media offer mobility and flexibility at the cost of being more susceptible to interference and distance limitations.

A link is also characterized by its transmission rate, often called bandwidth, which is the maximum rate at which it can carry data, typically measured in bits per second. A modern fiber optic backbone link in the network core might carry many gigabits per second, while a home WiFi access link might carry far less, and an individual cellular connection less still. This is exactly why the specific link connecting your device matters so much to your everyday experience: the same web server can be reached over a fast fiber link or a slow cellular link, and the transmission rate of whichever link you are using directly shapes how quickly data arrives.

Consider a worked example that threads together links across the whole path introduced in the previous two sections. Your laptop connects to your home router over a WiFi link, an unguided medium. Your home router connects to your internet service provider, often over a guided medium like coaxial or fiber cable. Within the provider's network core, data travels over high capacity fiber optic backbone links between routers. Eventually, on the far side, another access link, again possibly guided fiber or copper, connects into the destination server's data center. Every single hop along that entire journey, from your laptop to the destination server, depends on some communication link physically or wirelessly carrying the data from one node to the next.

Because every connection in a network, at the edge or in the core, is ultimately a link joining exactly two nodes, communication links are the literal infrastructure that turns a collection of independent nodes into an actual network capable of carrying traffic anywhere within it.
